definitions.definition: A made-up Latin-like word meaning 'two views' or 'double sight' — the idea of looking at something from two independent angles.
definitions.example: Like checking your answer to a math problem by solving it two different ways without peeking at the other method.

definitions.definition: Latin for 'therefore I am' — a famous phrase from philosopher René Descartes meaning 'I think, therefore I exist.'
definitions.example: Like saying 'I doubt, so I must be real.'

definitions.definition: The particular viewpoint or set of assumptions through which you see and interpret things.
definitions.example: Wearing blue sunglasses makes everything look blue — your lens is how you see the world.

definitions.definition: The system of methods and principles used to do a particular study or research.
definitions.example: A recipe for how to do science — step-by-step rules for getting reliable answers.

definitions.definition: When separate things come together to the same point or conclusion.
definitions.example: Two friends who don't talk to each other both guess the same number — that's convergence.

definitions.definition: Turned into a clear, written, step-by-step system or rule.
definitions.example: Turning a cool trick you discovered into a written magic routine with instructions.

definitions.definition: Expressed clearly in words.
definitions.example: Instead of just pointing, you say 'the red car on the left.'

definitions.definition: The ability of an AI to think through a problem on its own without help or hints from others.
definitions.example: Like a student who solves a test question without looking at anyone else's paper.

definitions.definition: Not recognizing the true worth or importance of something.
definitions.example: Thinking a $100 bill is only worth $10.

definitions.definition: Systems or setups designed to make AIs argue with each other to reach agreement.
definitions.example: Like a formal debate club where two teams argue a topic and then a judge picks a winner.

definitions.definition: Unfair preferences or slants that make you see things in a distorted way.
definitions.example: Only believing news from one website because you like that site, ignoring others.

definitions.definition: Agreement that happens naturally without being pushed or arranged.
definitions.example: Two friends independently decide to wear the same color shirt without planning it.

definitions.definition: Agreement that is deliberately created by a process, not naturally occurring.
definitions.example: A teacher making all students agree on an answer by having them discuss until they give up and agree.

definitions.definition: Different in kind or type, not just in amount.
definitions.example: An apple and an orange are qualitatively different — not just more or less of the same thing.

definitions.definition: Involving multiple AI systems working together or interacting.
definitions.example: A team of robot players in a video game, each with its own job.

definitions.definition: Repeatedly improving something by making small changes each time.
definitions.example: Editing an essay over and over, each time fixing a few mistakes.

definitions.definition: A small test to show that an idea or method can work in real life.
definitions.example: Building a tiny model bridge to see if the design holds before building the real one.

definitions.definition: A check to see how well the U.S. Constitution is being followed, using a specific method.
definitions.example: Like a report card for the Constitution, grading how much it's still in effect.

definitions.definition: Total or combined scores from multiple sources.
definitions.example: Adding up all your quiz grades to get a final average.

definitions.definition: A way of judging something based on what the original writers meant, not on later interpretations.
definitions.example: If a law says 'no vehicles in the park,' the author-intent standard asks 'what did they mean by vehicle?' not 'what does vehicle mean today?'

definitions.definition: A result that is very different from all the others.
definitions.example: In a class where most students score 70-80, one student scoring 100 is an outlier.

definitions.definition: Rules that would prove a scientific idea is wrong if they happen.
definitions.example: If you claim 'all swans are white,' then finding one black swan is a falsification criterion.

definitions.definition: Agreeing with someone just to please them, not because you truly agree.
definitions.example: Laughing at a unfunny joke because the boss told it.
definitions.first_appearance: Section 1: The Problem with Making Things Agree

definitions.definition: An argument that goes in a circle, using its conclusion as proof of itself.
definitions.example: Saying 'I'm right because I'm always right' is circular.
definitions.first_appearance: Section 1: The Problem with Making Things Agree

definitions.definition: Assumes something is true before having proof.
definitions.example: Saying 'stop beating your dog' presupposes you have a dog and beat it.
definitions.first_appearance: Section 1: The Problem with Making Things Agree

definitions.definition: The most important parts of the Constitution that protect personal freedoms.
definitions.example: Like the main pillars holding up a building — if they crack, the whole thing might fall.
definitions.first_appearance: Section 3: Proof of Concept — Four AIs, One Constitution

definitions.definition: Deliberately and methodically opposed or weakened over time.
definitions.example: If someone slowly removes bricks from a wall one by one, they are systematically counteracting the wall.
definitions.first_appearance: Section 3: Proof of Concept — Four AIs, One Constitution

definitions.definition: Changes to the Constitution that set up how the government works, not what rights people have.
definitions.example: Rules about how to count votes or how to pass a law.
definitions.first_appearance: Section 3: Proof of Concept — Four AIs, One Constitution

definitions.definition: Still whole and not broken or changed.
definitions.example: A toy that hasn't been played with and still has all its parts.
definitions.first_appearance: Section 3: Proof of Concept — Four AIs, One Constitution

definitions.definition: Worn away or weakened gradually.
definitions.example: A cliff slowly worn down by waves over many years.
definitions.first_appearance: Section 3: Proof of Concept — Four AIs, One Constitution

definitions.definition: The set of rules and principles that courts use to make decisions.
definitions.example: Like a playbook for judges: 'if this happens, then that rule applies.'
definitions.first_appearance: Section 3: Proof of Concept — Four AIs, One Constitution

definitions.definition: When information from one source accidentally gets into another, ruining independence.
definitions.example: If you tell one friend the answer and they tell another, that's cross-contamination.

definitions.definition: A set of clear rules or standards for grading something.
definitions.example: A checklist a teacher uses to grade an essay: 'spelling, grammar, ideas.'

definitions.definition: A detailed plan or set of steps to follow in a specific situation.
definitions.example: A fire drill protocol: 'stop, drop, and roll.'

definitions.definition: A hidden factor that confuses or mixes up the results of an experiment.
definitions.example: If you test whether coffee makes you alert, but everyone who drinks coffee also sleeps more, sleep is a confound.

definitions.definition: A result caused by the method itself, not by what you're studying.
definitions.example: A smudge on a microscope slide that looks like a tiny creature but is just dirt.

definitions.definition: Deep knowledge about a specific subject or field.
definitions.example: A chef has domain expertise in cooking; a doctor has it in medicine.

definitions.definition: Whether a finding from one situation applies to many other situations.
definitions.example: If a medicine works on mice, does it also work on humans? That's generalizability.

definitions.definition: Repeating an experiment to see if you get the same results.
definitions.example: Baking the same cake recipe twice to make sure it turns out the same.
